blocks.text: You see how uncertainly Bochart wavers between the pelican and the bittern. Nor would I think that anything certain can be put forward today about the bird קאת. [III, 48] For the ancient interpreters disagree; the etymology fits several birds; and what occurs in the Hebrew Codex about קאת is not so peculiar to one particular genus of birds that, among very different ones, no room for doubt is left. For there are many water birds (if indeed קאת is a water bird) which inhabit marshy deserts and utter a cry that is either plaintive and moaning or dreadful and clanging (Oedmann, moreover, says nothing about the voice of his Pelecanus graculus). — Among the Arabs, كعيت [kuʿayt] also occurs among the names of the nightingale. Hence Velthusen, in Part 2 of the Symbolae Kilonienses, edited in the vernacular by Cramer (Beyträge zur Beförderung theologischer und anderer nützlicher Kenntnisse), thinks that the Hebrew קאת is to be interpreted in Ps. CII, 7. as the solitary nightingale, and in Esaj. XXXIV, 11. and Zeph. II, 14. as the phoenicurus or ruticilla [redstart] (rossignol de muraille, de roc, ou de rocher, see Salerne, Ornithol. p. 233), which nests in the hollows of walls and of the back parts of houses, where people are less frequent (see Jonston, Theatr. animall., Frankfurt 1755, vol. 1, p. 125). But although the Arabs sometimes put the letter ك for the Hebrew ק (as in ضحك [ḍaḥika], Hebr. צחק, and كدر [kadira], Hebr. קדר), and ع for the Hebrew א (as كعب [kaʿaba], Hebr. כעב and כאב, he filled), such examples are nevertheless rare, and it is quite unusual for both Hebrew letters ק and א to stand in one and the same word for the Arabic ك and ع. — Jo. Christoph. Doederlein, in his Scholia on Psalm. CII, 7., explains קאת as the viverra Zibetha or wild cat, comparing the Arabic قط البر [qiṭṭ al-barr], i.e. wild cat, in Forsskål, Descript. Animall. p. 1, no. 7, letter b. But, to say nothing of the fact that the Hebrew קאת has nothing in common with the Arabic قط [qiṭṭ] except the sound, one cannot think of a mammalian quadruped for the reason that קאת appears among the birds in Levit. XI, 18. and Deut. XIV, 17.
